- Maternal tachycardia (110 bpm) and hypotension (90/60 mmHg) — signs of hypovolemic shock  
- Gestational age 38 weeks with prior cesarean delivery (major risk factor for scar rupture)  
- Uterine exam reveals no contractions — argues against ongoing labor and supports rupture occurring *after* contraction cessation  

[GAPS]  
- Baseline hemoglobin (to confirm acute drop)  
- Fibrinogen level (critical for assessing DIC risk in abruption, but diagnosis does not depend on it)  
- Placental location/margin on ultrasound (to definitively exclude placenta previa — though not suggested clinically)  
- Confirmation of fetal viability status post-decelerations (e.g., absence of baseline variability, acidosis on scalp pH or cord gas — not yet obtained due to urgency)  

[ESCALATION]  
- Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): Would require *abnormal fibrinogen (<200 mg/dL), elevated D-dimer, thrombocytopenia, or prolonged PT/aPTT* — none currently present.  
- Amniotic fluid embolism: Would require *sudden onset of hypoxia, coagulopathy, and cardiovascular collapse* — but here, bleeding and pain preceded shock, and coagulation is intact so far; no respiratory findings reported.  
- Aortic or iliac artery rupture: Would require *pulsatile abdominal mass, back/flank pain, or CT-confirmed vascular injury* — not supported by any data.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute placental abruption with concurrent complete uterine rupture at prior cesarean scar.
